title: Spin-polarized tunneling from a Kondo insulator: equilibrium surface magnetism versus magneto-electric response in SmB$_6$
abstract: We theoretically analyze the spin-polarized tunneling between SmB$_6$ tip and the bicollinear antiferromagnet Fe$_{1+x}$Te. The emergence of magnetic contrast in tunneling requires time-reversal symmetry breaking on the surface of the tip. The magnetic contrast part of the tunneling conductance then has two contributions: the first one originates from the magnetic moment due to the equilibrium long-range order on the surface, while the other is governed by the magnetic moment induced by the electric field of the junction through the surface magneto-electric effect. We show that the ratio of the equilibrium moment to the response extracted near zero bias equals, up to the sign, twice the bias at which the contrast changes sign, independently of the relative strength of the two mechanisms, so that this ratio itself does not measure the strength of the magneto-electric effect. We find that within the experimental energy window $|eV|\lesssim10$~meV the {bias-dependent} field-induced contribution is at most a few percent of the equilibrium one, and the two become comparable only at biases of order $100$~meV or higher. The ratio of the field-induced to the equilibrium contribution is inversely proportional to the distance between the tip and the substrate.
summary: This theoretical work investigates spin-polarized tunneling from the Kondo insulator $	ext{SmB}_6$ to separate the effects of intrinsic surface magnetism from field-induced magneto-electric coupling. By analyzing the tunneling conductance, the authors show that at low biases, the equilibrium magnetic order dominates the observed contrast, suggesting that the magneto-electric effect only becomes comparable at much higher bias voltages.
main_problem: The paper theoretically analyzes spin-polarized tunneling from a Kondo insulator ($	ext{SmB}_6$) to distinguish between the contribution of equilibrium surface magnetism and the magneto-electric response.
main_result: Within small bias windows ($|eV| \lesssim 10 	ext{ meV}$), the field-induced magneto-electric contribution is found to be negligible compared to the equilibrium contribution, which primarily dictates the energy dependence and bias reversal of the magnetic contrast.
method: The analysis uses linear response theory and perturbation theory applied to the tunneling conductance, expanding the spin-resolved spectral function to first order in the electric field.
model_or_system: The system involves spin-polarized tunneling between an $	ext{SmB}_6$ tip (a Kondo insulator candidate) and an $	ext{Fe}_{1+x}	ext{Te}$ substrate. The theory models the magnetic contrast using an eight-orbital description for $	ext{SmB}_6$.
key_observables: Magnetic contrast in the tunneling conductance, the ratio of equilibrium moment to field-induced response, and the bias dependence of the contrast.
important_parameters: Bias voltage ($V$), tip-substrate distance ($d$), and energy scales ($\sim 10 	ext{ meV}$ vs. $\sim 100 	ext{ meV}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the electric field perturbation is small compared to the static contact potential, and that the energy dependence of the spectral function is smooth over the apex structure energy scale.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates how time-reversal symmetry breaking causes the apex states to split, leading to a bias-dependent tunneling contrast that changes sign.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical context (spin-polarized tunneling, TRSB), derives the theoretical framework by expanding the spectral function to linear order in the electric field, and then calculates and compares the magnitude of the equilibrium versus the field-induced contributions.
why_interesting: The detailed separation of equilibrium magnetic order from field-induced magneto-electric effects in a strongly correlated material like a Kondo insulator provides a rigorous theoretical tool for interpreting complex transport measurements in correlated electron systems.
